constructionSpecial.quantumTitleLine2: construction contracts: a Quantum Claim guide
constructionSpecial.quantumIntro: Quantum claims on overseas construction projects can range from tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars. Based on standard forms such as FIDIC and JCT and common-law damages principles, here are the 7 claim types contractors raise most often and how they are typically valued.

item1.title: Contractor's claim vs Variation
item1.desc: The two contractual routes to monetary compensation are valued differently: a Contractor's claim is assessed on a loss-and-expense or cost basis, while a Variation is valued using contract rates or fair rates and prices.
points: Check the scope difference between 'loss and expense' and 'cost'
Assess whether expenditure incurred on or off the site is recoverable
Keep contemporary records and a project cost ledger up to date

item2.title: Valuing Variations
item2.desc: Valuation of Variations, including design changes, depends on differences between the bill of quantities and rate schedules, errors in contract rates, and changes in the character and conditions of the work.
points: Check whether applying the contract rate produces an unfair result for either party
Confirm whether the same valuation rule applies to omitted work as to added work
Assess recoverability of site overheads and progress disruption caused by the Variation

item3.title: Disruption claims
item3.desc: Raised when productivity falls below plan due to an Employer-risk event. Distinct from delay claims, and record-keeping is often decisive.
points: Measured Mile analysis — compare against an unimpacted period
Earned Value Method (EVM) and industry-study benchmarking
Total cost / modified total cost methods should be a last resort

item4.title: On-site overhead (prolongation) claims
item4.desc: Claims for site overheads such as labour and rental costs incurred because the works ran longer than the contract period.
points: Daily overhead rate method vs resource-by-resource analysis
Check for concurrent delay and avoid double recovery
Non-critical delay is generally excluded from prolongation costs

item5.title: Off-site overhead, profit & loss-of-profit claims
item5.desc: Claims for head-office overheads, contractual profit margin, and loss of profit from opportunities missed elsewhere due to an Employer-risk delay.
points: Check the preconditions before applying formulae such as Hudson, Emden or Eichleay
Actual head-office costs incurred to support the dispute should be proven separately
Causation between the delay and the lost opportunity must be established

item6.title: Back charge claims
item6.desc: Claims to recover costs the contractor incurred in place of a subcontractor or vendor due to their defect or breach.
points: Confirm the cost was actually, necessarily and reasonably incurred
Establish the subcontractor's responsibility under the subcontract
Confirm reasonable notice to cure was given before the cost was incurred

item7.title: Termination account claims
item7.desc: The FIDIC termination routes — termination for Contractor default, for the Employer's convenience, or for Employer default — each require a different set of account items.
points: Compare the final account against the cost of completion by a replacement contractor
Confirm which heads of compensation apply on a termination for convenience
Check whether liquidated damages provisions still apply after termination

quantumCautions: Both factual causation and legal causation (foreseeability) must be established.
Check the duty to mitigate and any betterment deduction in advance.
Global claims — lumping losses together without linking them to individual causes — weaken proof of causation.
Maintaining contemporary records consistently strengthens your position in litigation or arbitration.
constructionSpecial.quantumDisclaimer: This guide summarizes general information drawn from international construction quantum claim literature and does not substitute for legal advice on a specific matter.

immigration.subtitle: Working with a network of New York immigration attorneys, we build approval strategies even for low investment amounts or challenging business types.

requirements.heading: Core E-2 Visa Requirements
requirements.item1: Must be a national of a treaty country (80+ countries across Europe, Africa, Asia, South America, the Middle East, North America)
requirements.item2: Must own at least 50% of the E-2 company
requirements.item3: Must make a "Substantial" investment — funds must be actually spent and "at risk", not sitting in a bank account
requirements.item4: Source of funds can be any legitimate source (personal savings, gift, sale of a house, loan)
requirements.item5: Business cannot be marginal — it must support hiring U.S. employees
requirements.item6: Business must be real and operating (or ready to operate once the visa is granted): signed lease, entity formed, website live, customer contracts, licenses acquired
requirements.item7: You must solely develop and direct the enterprise as an active investor (ownership greater than 50%)
requirements.item8: You must intend to return to your home country when the E-2 visa expires
requirements.item9: You can start a new business or buy an existing one (escrow considerations apply when buying)

validity.heading: Visa Validity
validity.item1: Valid from 3 months up to 5 years, depending on the strength of the case as assessed by the officer
validity.item2: I-94 allows entry and work in increments of up to 2 years

investment.heading: How much investment is enough?
investment.item1: The investment must be "substantial" — there is no fixed statutory minimum
investment.item2: In practice, the investment would normally be greater than $50,000
investment.item3: The money must actually be spent, and the amount needed depends on the type of business
investment.item4: Proportionality test (start-up): the amount invested versus the usual cost of establishing that type of business
investment.item5: Proportionality test (buying a business): purchase price versus the fair market value of the business
investment.item6: Evidence that you invested close to 100% — CPA letters and industry cost articles help substantiate this

lowInvestment.heading: Strategies for a Low Investment Amount
lowInvestment.item1: Stress other positive factors: experience, employee hires, type of business
lowInvestment.item2: Obtain contracts or letters of intent from clients
lowInvestment.item3: Obtain a Chamber of Commerce letter
lowInvestment.item4: Highlight any ongoing company activity or sales
lowInvestment.item5: Draft a strong, detailed business plan
lowInvestment.item6: Hire U.S. employees prior to applying
lowInvestment.item7: Consider a CPA letter verifying the investment

expendituresGood.heading: Strong, Qualifying Expenditures
expendituresGood.item3: Inventory (can be shipped from another country; doesn't need to be purchased in the U.S.)
expendituresGood.item6: Employee payroll or independent contractor payments
expendituresGood.item8: Lease payments (only amounts actually paid, e.g. prepaid months)

expendituresWeak.heading: Weak, Non-Qualifying Expenditures
expendituresWeak.item1: Flights (unless tied to a specific conference or business activity)

denials.heading: Common Reasons for Denial
denials.item2: Nature of the business (viewed as passive or speculative)
denials.item4: A similar business operating in the home country without employees
denials.item5: Concern over whether the business will create jobs for U.S. workers
denials.item7: Requirements were not met at the time of filing

consulting.title: Consulting Businesses
consulting.desc: Theoretically a very low investment can start a consulting business, but you must show you are "committed to successfully operating the enterprise." Use industry cost articles to show you've spent well above typical start-up costs, and spread spending across a wide range of categories — office space, equipment, marketing, and hiring.

realEstate.title: Real Estate Investments
realEstate.desc: Simply purchasing a property under an LLC does not qualify. You must show the company is a real, operating enterprise — not an idle, speculative investment held for appreciation. Viable formats include a brokerage firm, a property management company, renovation/construction, or large-scale house flipping.

trading.title: Equity Trading Companies
trading.desc: Placing a personal stock portfolio under an LLC (day trading, personal investing) will not qualify. Clients must go beyond friends and family, and the business must show hiring plans and proper licensing as a genuinely active enterprise.

cta.heading: See if your case fits the E-2 visa
cta.desc: Even with a low investment amount or a challenging business type, the right strategy can improve approval odds. Book an initial consultation to review your investment amount, source of funds, and business plan.
